name: Dong Son culture
info: The Đông Sơn culture was a Bronze Age culture centred on the Red River Delta of northern Vietnam (c. 1000 BCE – 1st century CE), famed for bronze drums that are found across Southeast Asia and southern China.

facts.homeland: Northern Vietnam, centred on the Red River Delta; named after the village of Đông Sơn in Thanh Hóa province; related finds in Laos, Malaysia and the Chinese provinces of Yunnan, Guangxi and Fujian; sites include Đông Sơn and Núi Nấp.
facts.period: c. 1000 BCE – 1st century CE; it grew out of the Gò Mun culture and marks the culmination of the Bronze Age and the opening of the Iron Age; its bronze drum culture disappears after the Han conquest of the Red River Plain.
facts.known: Heger I bronze kettledrums decorated with a sun, frogs, warships and feather-headdressed warriors; lost-wax bronze casting; rice farming; water buffalo and pigs; fishing and sailing in long dugout canoes; bronze daggers
facts.sources: Excavations at Đông Sơn village from 1924; the bronze drums and analyses of their metal; early Chinese texts such as the Shiben; ancient DNA and skull studies; the history of the Vietic languages.

t: Đông Sơn is an archaeological culture named after a village in Thanh Hóa province, Vietnam, where bronze drums were first excavated in 1924; it centred on the Red River Delta.
Its people farmed rice, kept water buffalo and pigs, fished and sailed long dugout canoes, and cast bronze drums decorated with scenes of their world.
Who the Đông Sơn people were is debated: some link them to the Vietic ancestors of the Vietnamese, others see several peoples who shared one trading culture.

sections.origins:
The Đông Sơn culture, also called the Dongsonian or Lạc Việt culture, is a Bronze Age archaeological culture centred on the Red River Delta of northern Vietnam. It takes its name, “East Mountain”, from the village of Đông Sơn in Thanh Hóa province, where bronze drums were first excavated in 1924. Artefacts closely related to it date from about 1000 BCE to the 1st century CE.

The excavations began after a fisherman, Nguyễn Văn Lắm, told the École française d’Extrême-Orient in Hanoi that he had come across large quantities of bronze objects. Scattered Đông Sơn bronzes are said to have been found as early as the Lý dynasty (1010–1225), and in 1898 they drew the attention of the Austrian archaeologist Franz Heger, who created a classification of bronze drums; the drums of Đông Sơn are his Heger I type. The first literary mention of bronze drums is in the Chinese text Shiben of the 3rd century BCE.

The culture grew out of the Gò Mun culture and marks the culmination of the Bronze Age and the opening stage of the Iron Age. Scholars once traced bronze casting to China, but finds made in Isan, Thailand, in the 1970s showed that casting either began first in Southeast Asia or developed there independently. The Đông Sơn bronze industry is therefore seen as local in origin rather than brought by migrants from China. Pottery and bronzes in a similar style from Thailand may be older still, possibly placing the culture’s ancestor in the region by the 4th or 5th millennium BCE.
sections.society:
The Đông Sơn people were skilled rice farmers who kept water buffalo and pigs, fished, and sailed in long dugout canoes. The pestle, the oar and a pan for cooking sticky rice have been called the main characteristics of the culture, and the linguist Ferlus traced new words for them in the Vietic languages.

The bronze drums were used in war, when “the chief summons the warriors of the tribe by beating the drum”, in mourning and at feasts, and the scenes cast on them suggest that Đông Sơn leaders had access to bronze founders of great skill. A single large drum demanded a great deal of metal: the Cổ Loa drum, weighing 72 kilograms, would have needed between 1 and 7 tonnes of copper ore to be smelted.

Vietnamese historians attribute the culture to the early states of Văn Lang and Âu Lạc. The drums themselves picture daily life and ritual: drummers and other musicians, warriors, the processing of rice, birds, deer and war vessels. Musicians on several drums, including the Ngoc Lu drum, seem to play the khene, an instrument closely associated with Lao speakers.
sections.beliefs:
Little is known directly of Đông Sơn beliefs. What can be said comes from the bronze drums, their decoration and the occasions on which they were used, and any reading of them is inference.

The decoration of the Heger I drums is the richest evidence. At the centre of the drumhead is a sun, and around it run rings of warships and of warriors in feather headdresses; models of stylised frogs sit on the drumhead. The frogs and the radiating sun recur on the larger, plainer Heger II drums too. What the sun, the frogs and the processions of boats and warriors meant to their makers is not recorded.

The drums’ uses point to ceremony. They sounded at mourning and at feasts as well as in war, which suggests that they had a part in rites for the dead and in communal celebrations.
sections.arts:
The Đông Sơn people were skilled bronze casters, as the drums found widely through northern Vietnam and in Yunnan and Guangxi show. Bronze drums were made in large numbers in northern Vietnam, Laos and parts of Yunnan. The founders used lost-wax casting, a technique based on Chinese practice, but the scenes on the drums are local: drummers and other musicians, warriors, rice processing, birds, deer, war vessels and geometric designs.

Heger I drums carry intricate decoration around a central sun, with model frogs on the drumhead. Heger II drums, also called Li Lao drums, share the frogs and radiating sun but are much larger and decorated more plainly. According to the Lịch Sử Cổ Đại Việt Nam, the high lead content of Đông Sơn bronzes is what sets them apart from Chinese bronzes, and drums from Guangxi and Yunnan contain less lead than those of the Red River Plain.

Other bronzes show wider links: some Đông Sơn bronze daggers closely resemble Scytho-Siberian styles.
sections.exchange:
Đông Sơn-style objects spread widely. Artefacts closely related to the culture, or believed to belong to it, have been found in Malaysia, Laos and the Chinese provinces of Yunnan, Guangxi and Fujian, and its influence reached maritime Southeast Asia. The lower lead content of drums from Guangxi and Yunnan suggests that drum-making spread outwards from the Red River Plain. The close relationship with the Dian culture of Yunnan has led some to see the two as variants of one culture: Alice Yao argues that both belong to a single material phenomenon represented by more than 250 bronze drums, and differ in name only because of the nationality of the archaeologists.

Who the Đông Sơn people were is debated. They spoke either Austroasiatic or Northern Tai languages, or were Austroasiatic speakers in close contact and mixing with Tai speakers. Ancient DNA shows that the Red River Delta’s earlier inhabitants were mainly Austroasiatic: people buried at Mán Bạc, a site of the Phùng Nguyên culture, are close to modern Austroasiatic speakers such as the Khmer and Mlabri, while those of the Đông Sơn site of Núi Nấp show mixed ancestry. One study models the Núi Nấp people as about 65% Dushan-related and 35% northern East Asian-related.

Ferlus (2009) argued from the Vietic words for the pestle, oar and sticky-rice pan, and from where Northern Vietic is spoken today, that the culture was Vietic and its people the direct ancestors of the Vietnamese. Historians including Keith W. Taylor, Nguyen Phuong and John D. Phan answer that there is no actual evidence for this; Phan notes that Đông Sơn-style artefacts occur as far afield as Malaysia and Fujian and probably belonged to several distinct peoples who traded with each other.
sections.legacy:
The Đông Sơn culture ended with Han Chinese rule. In Vietnam, its material evidence, such as the bronze drums, disappears at the time of the Trưng sisters’ defeat and the appearance of Han material culture, which suggests that the sisters led a failed indigenous uprising. After the Han general Ma Yuan conquered the Red River Plain, the bronze drum culture disappeared.

More than 120 Han brick tombs in the Red River region point to growing Chinese migration into the area, or to strong cultural influence of the newcomers on the local people, and the earliest Sino-Vietnamese loanwords date from around this time. The culture’s identity remains a live question: Vietnamese historians link it with the states of Văn Lang and Âu Lạc and some linguists with the ancestors of the Vietnamese, while other historians see no evidence for that link.

The drums remain its best-known legacy. The name Đông Sơn is still used by some as a catch-all term for bronze kettledrums across southern China and Southeast Asia, while others keep it for the Heger I type alone. Displays of Đông Sơn drum surfaces can be seen in several of Vietnam’s cultural institutions.

summary: The Đông Sơn culture was a Bronze Age culture centred on the Red River Delta of northern Vietnam from about 1000 BCE to the 1st century CE. Its people farmed rice, kept buffalo and pigs, fished and sailed dugout canoes, and cast bronze drums decorated with suns, frogs, warships and feathered warriors. Its drums and influence spread across Southeast Asia and southern China, and it faded after the Han conquest of the Red River Plain.

notes: The saved article is short (about 10 KB); the beliefs and arts sections are shorter than the 1,700-character target rather than padded, and beliefs is labelled as inference from the drums throughout.
The article speaks of “Michael Churchman” for the 120 Han brick tombs, but its bibliography lists Catherine Churchman (2016); I left the name out of the text.

The bibliography gives Taylor 1983 as “The Birth of the Vietnam”; I wrote the real title, The Birth of Vietnam. Yao (2017, Springer) may be an encyclopedia chapter rather than a book; the article gives no more detail.

The article’s wording on Franz Heger (1898) is unclear (“claimed to be rediscovered … and later, Austrian archaeologist Franz Heger in 1898, who created a classification of bronze drums”); I kept the event vague. The Lý dynasty rediscovery is given as a claim (“said to”).

The article gives the culture’s end both as the 1st century CE and (for Vietnamese historians’ view) 1 BCE; no date is given for the Trưng sisters or Ma Yuan, so I dated that event only to the 1st century CE. Start and end kept.

Ferlus and Nguyen Phuong are given as in the article (no first name for Ferlus; Nguyen Phuong without diacritics). The khene link to Lao speakers is stated as the article does; the genetic findings are as the article reports them.
